title: Chapter 116
content:
The more Lan Wangji kept up that deadpan, upright act, the more Wei Wuxian’s fingers itched to stir the pot.

He tapped a fingernail lightly against the unglazed pottery bowl. The small, sharp click was so faint only the two of them could hear it, but Lan Wangji’s gaze drifted sideways by a hair.

Wei Wuxian knew that no matter how impeccably polite Lan Wangji looked facing forward, those pale eyes tracked his every breath. Grinning inwardly, Wei Wuxian lifted the little black bowl as if taking a drink, turning it slowly in his hands until his mouth lined up with the exact spot Lan Wangji’s lips had pressed. Slowly, deliberately, he sealed his own lips over the cold rim.

Across the tiny gap between their tables, Lan Wangji’s hands remained neatly folded over his lap. His posture didn't shift by a millimeter, but beneath the immaculate white sweep of his wide sleeves, his fingers curled tight into his palms.

A thrill of smug delight bubbled up Wei Wuxian’s spine. Getting ahead of himself, he started leaning sideways to drape his weight onto Lan Wangji’s shoulder, right on cue—

Ahem!

A venomous, dry cough barked from the head of the hall. Lan Qiren was glaring holes through him. Wei Wuxian snapped his spine straight in a blink, plastering on the most devout, textbook posture he could muster.

Once the soup bowls were cleared and a respectable silence had passed, the main dishes finally arrived.

Three tiny porcelain dishes landed on each low table. Plain green leaves, boiled white roots, and watery tofu—a depressing spread identical down to the last scallion to the slop he’d endured as a guest disciple all those years ago. Aside from somehow tasting even more bitter, the menu hadn't evolved a single inch. Between his Yunmeng roots and his personal nature, Wei Wuxian liked his food heavy, drenched in chili oil, and loaded with meat; staring down this monk’s diet killed whatever appetite he had. He shovelled it down without chewing, entirely numb to whatever he was swallowing. The whole time, Lan Qiren’s eyes darted his way like daggers, practically burning with the urge to bark his name and throw him out into the rain. But Wei Wuxian was behaving so uncharacteristically well that the old man found zero excuses to pounce, left only to simmer in bitter frustration.

After choking down a meal with all the flavor of wet paper, the servants swept the dishes away. As was customary, Lan Xichen took the floor to deliver a calm recap of recent clan affairs.

Yet before he was even a few sentences in, Wei Wuxian could tell the sect leader was completely out of it. He was distant, his focus drifting like smoke, and he even managed to mix up the locations of two different night-hunts without catching his own blunder. Lan Qiren’s scowl deepened with every slip, his goat-like beard puffing with agitated huffs until he finally cut in, calling the gathering to a blunt, hasty close.

A stiff beginning, a suffocating meal, and an awkward finish. Trapped in solemn silence for nearly two hours with no spicy food and certainly no music or revelry, Wei Wuxian felt as though a colony of phantom fleas had set up camp under his skin. To make matters worse, the second they stood up, Lan Qiren barked at both brothers to follow him to his quarters—clearly gearing up to lecture the Twin Jades of Gusu in a two-for-one special.

Left with nobody to tease, Wei Wuxian wandered aimlessly down the covered verandas. Catching sight of a few juniors strolling in small groups ahead, he opened his mouth to call them over for a little fun.

The moment Lan Sizhui and Lan Jingyi clocked his face, their eyes widened in absolute horror. They spun on their heels and bolted in the opposite direction.

Wei Wuxian didn't take offense; he knew the drill. Hands tucked behind his back, he sauntered into a quiet, shaded grove of pine trees. Sure enough, after a few minutes, several white-robed figures came creeping out from the shadows like guilty thieves.

"Senior Wei, please don't take it personally!" Lan Sizhui pleaded under his breath. "The Teacher gave strict orders—anyone caught talking to you has to copy the entire Clan Rules from start to finish..."

To every generation of Gusu Lan disciples, "The Teacher" was an absolute title, reserved solely for Lan Qiren.

Wei Wuxian puffed out his chest, utterly unbothered. "No sweat, I already figured. Your grandmaster’s been trying to protect his house from fire, theft, and Wei Wuxian since before you were born. Has it worked yet? Not once! The poor old man’s just heartbroken that his prize-winning cabbage got thoroughly uprooted and eaten by a wild pig. Can't blame him for having a little temper, hahahaha!"

Lan Jingyi stared at him, speechlessly horrified by the metaphor, while Lan Sizhui offered an awkward, pained little chuckle.

Once he finished laughing, Wei Wuxian asked, "By the way, you kids were doing handstands earlier for night-hunting with Wen Ning. How's he holding up?"

Lan Sizhui pondered for a moment. "Hard to say. Probably lying low somewhere around the foot of the mountain until our next outing. Though... when we parted ways, Sect Leader Jiang seemed pretty furious..."

Wei Wuxian’s eyebrows shot up. "What?! Jiang Cheng? What was he doing there?"

"We'd invited Young Master Jin along on that hunt," Lan Sizhui explained sheepishly. "So..."

The picture snapped together instantly.

It didn't take a genius to work it out: Wen Ning had probably been tailing Jin Ling or the Lan boys from the shadows, ready to step in if their night-hunt went south. Meanwhile, Jiang Cheng had undoubtedly been creeping along behind his nephew as well, hovering like a helicopter parent terrified the boy would scrape a knee. Naturally, the two guardian angels had run right into each other in the middle of a crisis, sparking an explosive screaming match. A quick round of questions confirmed it, leaving Wei Wuxian torn between a groan and a laugh.

Sighing, he asked, "How are Jiang Cheng and Jin Ling doing lately?"

With Jin Guangyao dead, Jin Ling was the only direct heir left to claim the Lanling Jin Clan. But a flock of greedy branch-family elders had been circling like vultures, salivating at the sudden power vacuum. Jin Ling was barely a teenager, nowhere near seasoned enough to command a den of scheming vipers while the rest of the cultivation world pointed and laughed at their disgrace. In the end, Jiang Cheng had marched up the gilded steps of Koi Tower with Zidian crackling at his wrist, staring down every elder in the room until the boy was firmly planted on the clan leader's seat. Where things went from here was anyone's guess.

Lan Jingyi crossed his arms and huffed. "They seem fine to me. Sect Leader Jiang is still his usual charming self, threatening to break legs and whip people into next week. And the Young Mistress is worse than ever—used to be his uncle would snap at him once and he'd talk back three times. Now he talks back ten times!"

Lan Sizhui gently scolded him. "Jingyi, you shouldn't call people that behind their backs."

"Why not?" Jingyi retorted defensively. "I call him that to his face, too!"

Hearing that, Wei Wuxian quietly let out the breath he'd been holding.

He knew deep down that wasn't what he’d really been worried about, but if Jiang Cheng and Jin Ling were alive, kicking, and screaming at each other as usual, that was enough.

Dusting off his robes, he got to his feet. "Well, that sounds lively. Tell them to keep up the good work. You kids run along and play, I've got important business to attend to."

Lan Jingyi gave him a look of pure disdain. "You literally lounge around doing nothing all day in the Cloud Recesses! What business could you possibly have?!"

Wei Wuxian strolled away, waving a dismissive hand over his shoulder. "Tending to my cabbage!"

Having been dragged out of bed at an ungodly hour that morning, he headed straight back to the Jingshi, buried himself under the covers, and promptly went back to sleep. Flipping his day and night upside down came with a price: by the time he finally woke, twilight had already draped over the mountains, and dinner had long since passed. Shrugging off the hunger, he whiled away the hours digging through Lan Wangji's old calligraphy scrolls and personal writings, keeping one ear on the door. But as night crept in, his prize cabbage was still nowhere to be seen.

By then, his stomach was growling in earnest. A quick glance out the window told him curfew was already in effect. According to the mountain rules, unauthorized nighttime wandering was strictly prohibited, and scaling the walls to sneak out was an even graver offense. In the old days, Wei Wuxian wouldn't have given a damn about what was forbidden—if he was hungry, he ate; if he was sleepy, he crashed; if he was bored, he flirted; and if he got caught, he ran. But things were different now. If he broke the rules today, the elders wouldn't punish him; they'd put the penalty straight on Lan Wangji's tab. Sighing heavily, he curled back onto the floor, resigned to starve.

A soft rustle sounded from the porch, followed by the silent slide of the wooden lattice.

Lan Wangji was back.

Wei Wuxian dropped flat on the floor, playing dead.

Soft, familiar footsteps glided toward the low desk, setting something down without a word. Wei Wuxian had intended to keep up the dead-body routine, but the faint click of a lid lifting released a rich, mouthwatering cloud of chili oil and toasted spices, instantly obliterating the quiet scent of sandalwood in the room.

Wei Wuxian scrambled up like a starving demon. "Er-gege! I swear my life to you!"

Lan Wangji didn't bat an eye, calmly unloading the lacquered tiers of the food carrier onto the desk. Wei Wuxian drifted over like a hungry ghost, his eyes practically gleaming red at the sight of five or six porcelain plates drenched in fiery scarlet sauces. "Hanguang-jun, you shouldn't have! Look at you, bringing me takeout like an attentive husband! Tell me what chores you need done, I'm your man!"

Lan Wangji laid a pair of ivory chopsticks neatly across the porcelain bowl, murmuring flatly, "No talking while eating."

"You also say no talking in bed," Wei Wuxian shot back, snatching the chopsticks, "yet you don't seem to mind when I run my mouth all night long."

Lan Wangji cast a pointed look his way.

"Alright, alright, I'll shut up," Wei Wuxian laughed, sitting across from him. "Look at you, getting shy over every little thing even after all this time. That’s what I love about you. Did you grab this from that Hunan joint in Caiyi Town?"

Lan Wangji offered no answer, which Wei Wuxian took as full confirmation. He scooped up a bite, humming in pure bliss. "Glad to see they haven't gone out of business. Jiang Cheng and I used to crash there all the time—if we hadn't sneaked off to eat real food, I would've withered away during my guest disciple days. Now this is what a family banquet ought to look like."

Lan Wangji paused. "'We'?"

"Yeah, Jiang Cheng and me," Wei Wuxian said casually. "Sometimes Nie Huaisang and a few of the other guys tagged along."

Catching the sudden chill in the air, Wei Wuxian glanced up, a teasing grin spreading across his face. "What's with that look, Hanguang-jun? Don't tell me you forgot I invited you out with us back then! I was so eager, so persistent, practically begged you to come, and you turned your nose up at me every single time. One word from me and you'd glare daggers, shooting me down left and right. I haven't even brought that up to settle the score, and here you are sulking about it."

He scooted around the low desk, pressing his shoulder flush against Lan Wangji's. "Truth be told... I was on my best behavior tonight. I was so worried about breaking curfew and dragging your name through the mud that I starved in here like a good boy, waiting for you to come home. Who knew the spotless Hanguang-jun would break the rules himself just to fetch me a midnight snack? If your uncle ever finds out you snuck off the mountain after dark, his heart's going to seize up completely."

Lan Wangji lowered his arm, curling it smoothly around Wei Wuxian's waist. He didn't speak, but his fingers drifted absently across the curve of his hip. The heat of those broad palms radiated straight through the thin linen, burning warm against his skin.

Wei Wuxian leaned into the touch, whining softly, "Hanguang-jun, that bitter soup of yours ruined my tongue. My whole mouth tastes like medicine—I can't even enjoy this feast. What am I supposed to do?"

"One sip," Lan Wangji replied simply.

"Yeah, just one sip! But whoever brewed that cursed draught must have used ancient herbs with a vengeance. The bitterness is glued to the back of my throat. Come on, fix it. Tell me what to do."

A heavy silence lingered in the air.

"Neutralize it," Lan Wangji murmured softly.

Wei Wuxian batted his eyelashes, feigning deep curiosity. "And how do we do that?"

Lan Wangji tilted his chin up.

Their lips met in the dim candlelight, the faint, lingering trace of herbal bitterness sweetening into a deep, endless kiss.

When they finally broke apart for air, Wei Wuxian’s eyes were glassy, a breathless laugh escaping his throat. "Hanguang-jun... it just hit me. You drank two whole bowls of that stuff earlier. You should taste way more bitter than me."

"Mn."

"So why do you taste so sweet? It doesn't make sense."

Lan Wangji stared at him, his gaze dark and steady. "Eat your food."

He paused, his voice dropping an octave lower: "We will settle our business afterward."

Wei Wuxian’s smile turned thoroughly wicked. "Why wait? I say we eat the cabbage first."

Lan Wangji’s brow pinched in brief, genuine confusion over the sudden mention of greens, only for Wei Wuxian to burst into loud laughter, throwing both arms around his neck and hauling him straight down.

After all, a proper family feast was always best held behind closed doors.
